Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A single light-check search surfaced an ITU-sourced figure (via TheGlobalEconomy.com aggregator) of 9.3 kbit/s per internet user, but this is dated 2016 - the last year in the 2012-2016 series - and ITU appears to have discontinued regular per-country publication of this specific indicator since. Given the near-decade gap and Egypt's substantial subsequent expansion of subsea cable and internet capacity, this figure is too stale to assign a confident current-state code. Escalated from a simple Unknown confirmation to full path because the search returned a nominally authoritative (ITU) data point, but the evidence is not fit to score present-day bandwidth. Flagged for human review rather than guessing.
revised_comments: No current, reliable estimate of Egypt's international internet bandwidth per internet user is available. The most recent internationally comparable figure traceable to ITU data (9.3 kbit/s per user) dates to 2016 and is too dated to characterise the country's present-day international connectivity, particularly given subsequent growth in subsea cable capacity and internet uptake.

Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search surfaced GSMA Intelligence data (via DataReportal) showing 95.4% of Egypt's mobile connections were broadband-capable (3G/4G/5G) as of October 2025, and GSMA's Mobile Economy MENA reports project Egypt as one of the region's largest smartphone markets (~128-130 million smartphone connections forecast by 2030). This escalated the row to full path. No single source gives an exact 'smartphone share of connections' figure for Egypt specifically, so the broadband-connection share is used as the closest available proxy; band raised from Unknown to 5 (80%+) with medium confidence given the proxy nature of the metric.
revised_comments: Smartphone adoption in Egypt is high. GSMA Intelligence data reported via DataReportal indicate that 95.4 percent of Egypt's mobile connections were broadband-capable (3G, 4G or 5G) by late 2025, and GSMA's Mobile Economy Middle East & North Africa series ranks Egypt among the region's largest smartphone markets, with smartphone connections forecast to reach around 128-130 million by 2030.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search surfaced Egypt's regulator-published (EgyptERA) tiered residential tariff schedule (EGP 0.68/kWh for 0-50 kWh up to EGP 2.58/kWh above 1,000 kWh) and World Bank GNI per capita data (US$3,510, 2024), escalating the row to full path. However, calculating cost as a share of income is highly sensitive to the average monthly consumption assumed: historical estimates range from ~234 kWh/month (2016 World Bank-cited figure) to a considerably higher ~650 kWh/month in a 2026 study, and these produce estimated affordability shares anywhere from roughly 1% to 7% of GNI per capita - spanning the 'Moderate' to 'Expensive' bands. Given this sensitivity and the absence of a single authoritative affordability computation (e.g., from Enterprise Surveys or ESMAP) for Egypt, the code is not asserted and is flagged for human review.
revised_comments: Egypt applies a steeply tiered residential electricity tariff regulated by the Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA), ranging from EGP 0.68 per kWh for the lowest consumption bracket (0-50 kWh) up to EGP 2.58 per kWh for consumption above 1,000 kWh (2024-2026 schedules). Against a GNI per capita of around US$3,510 (World Bank, 2024), the share of household income spent on a basic electricity bundle is estimated at somewhere between roughly 1 and 7 percent, depending on the average monthly consumption assumed, placing affordability between moderate and expensive.

Definition: The country's e-government development level based on the UN E-Government Development Index (EGDI). This composite index measures online service delivery, telecommunications infrastructure, and human capital. Indicates the government's capacity to deliver digital public services.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search immediately surfaced the UN E-Government Survey 2024 (UN DESA), a clearly authoritative primary source, so the row was escalated to full path. The Survey gives Egypt an EGDI of 0.6699, ranked around 95th of 193 UN member states, in the 'H3' high-development rating class, placing Egypt above the global and African regional averages and among the top 100 countries for the first time in 2024 (alongside Morocco). Per the variable's scale, 0.6699 falls in the 0.65-0.79 (Very High) band, so the code is recalculated from 0 (Unknown) to 4.
revised_comments: Egypt's e-government development is assessed as very high under the UN E-Government Development Index (EGDI), scoring 0.6699 in the 2024 UN E-Government Survey (13th edition) and ranking around 95th out of 193 UN member states, placing it in the 'H3' high-development rating class. This score sits above both the global and African regional averages; 2024 marked Egypt's first appearance among the top 100 performers worldwide, alongside Morocco.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search immediately surfaced GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report, a clearly authoritative primary source for this indicator, escalating the row to full path. The 2024 edition (based on 2023 survey data) reports that 65% of men and 54% of women in Egypt use mobile internet - an 11-percentage-point gap - while mobile phone ownership overall is close to gender parity and narrowed further in the 2025 edition. Per the variable's scale, an 11pp gap falls in the 10-19% (Small gap) band, so the code is recalculated from 0 (Unknown) to 4.
revised_comments: There is a small gender gap in mobile internet use in Egypt. GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report (2024 edition, based on nationally representative 2023 survey data) finds that 65 percent of men and 54 percent of women in Egypt use mobile internet, an 11-percentage-point gap, while overall mobile phone ownership is close to gender parity and has continued to narrow in subsequent survey rounds.

Definition: The scale and quality of tertiary-level ICT and STEM education programmes available in the country, based on the number and quality of institutions offering ICT degrees, computer science programmes, and engineering courses relative to the population.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search surfaced the Global Knowledge Index (UNDP / Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum Knowledge Foundation, drawing on UNESCO UIS data), which reports Egypt's tertiary ICT graduates at 10.48% and STEM graduates at 20.76% of total tertiary graduates, ranked 79th of 123 countries on the ICT sub-index. This, combined with Egypt's large, long-established higher-education system (multiple major public universities plus private/international institutions offering computer science and engineering degrees), supports escalating from Unknown to a 'Good' (established institutions with diverse ICT programmes) rating. Confidence is medium because the source is a composite index rather than a single primary UNESCO figure, and the exact vintage of the underlying graduate data is not fully clear (GKI 2021 edition).
revised_comments: Egypt has a well-established tertiary ICT and STEM education base. According to the Global Knowledge Index, a composite drawing on UNESCO Institute for Statistics data, tertiary graduates from ICT programmes account for around 10.5 percent, and STEM graduates around 20.8 percent, of Egypt's total tertiary graduates, with Egypt ranked 79th of 123 countries on the ICT sub-index. This reflects a range of established public universities (including Cairo, Ain Shams and Alexandria universities) and private/international institutions (such as the American University in Cairo and the German University in Cairo) offering computer science, engineering and related ICT degree programmes.
